subject: disposition
justification: every intended dependency is implied by an adjudicated key and no intended multivalued dependency remains, with no candidate left unruled

subject: model
value: One row is the full plain-text extraction of exactly one catalogued PDF, held as a 1:1 extension of its documents row.
justification: The DDL is unambiguous: doc_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY REFERENCES documents(id) ON DELETE CASCADE. INTEGER PRIMARY KEY is the rowid, so it is non-null and unique in every legal state, and the FK plus cascade makes this a strict vertical partition of documents rather than an independent entity: 149 rows against 149 documents, one per document. The only dependency discovered is doc_id -> text, which is the PK dependency itself; the relation is 4NF with nothing to decompose. text is one archived document body (a whole extracted PDF), not several instances of one fact, and discovery raised no atomicity candidate for it. Scope is current-state because text is the extraction of the file presently at documents.path (all 149 rows have text_ok=1 and text_chars set); re-extracting a replaced PDF overwrites text under the same doc_id. There is no scan_id, version, or timestamp column, so the row asserts what the file contains now, not a history of extractions.

subject: doc_id
justification: named as an identifying key by the relation model. The DDL is unambiguous: doc_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY REFERENCES documents(id) ON DELETE CASCADE. INTEGER PRIMARY KEY is the rowid, so it is non-null and unique in every legal state, and the FK plus cascade makes this a strict vertical partition of documents rather than an independent entity: 149 rows against 149 documents, one per document. The only dependency discovered is doc_id -> text, which is the PK dependency itself; the relation is 4NF with nothing to decompose. text is one archived document body (a whole extracted PDF), not several instances of one fact, and discovery raised no atomicity candidate for it. Scope is current-state because text is the extraction of the file presently at documents.path (all 149 rows have text_ok=1 and text_chars set); re-extracting a replaced PDF overwrites text under the same doc_id. There is no scan_id, version, or timestamp column, so the row asserts what the file contains now, not a history of extractions.

subject: author
justification: The curated author field: a uniformly '; '-delimited list of the document's authors (e.g. id 8 'Nick Gurski; Niles Johnson; Angelica Osorno'). 98 of 149 values contain ';', none contain the word 'and', and only 2 contain a comma, so the delimiter is a deliberate normalisation, not prose punctuation. Each element is one author of one document: several instances of the same fact about the determinant, which is the definition of a repeating group. It belongs in a document_authors(doc_id, ordinal, author_name) child relation, which is also what any author query needs. Contrast original_author, the raw pdfinfo string it was normalised from, which is a single verbatim capture.

subject: inference_notes
justification: A free-text annotation on one document recording how its title, author, or year was established; 53 of 149 rows carry one, the rest are empty. '; ' here is overloaded rather than a list delimiter: id 194 uses it both between prose fragments and inside a trailing keyword run - 'Title/authors from first page; DOI 10.1134/S0081543815010198.; keywords: substitution tilings; aperiodic tilings; inductive rotation; limit-periodic tilings' - so splitting on it would cut a sentence and a keyword list into indistinguishable pieces. Many values are a single sentence with no delimiter at all (id 119 'Lab website capture, not an authored research paper.'; id 105 'Supplement/table PDF associated with IPC paper.'). This is one provenance/justification envelope about one row: long and structured, but a single value.

subject: inferred_author
justification: The inference pass's proposed author list for the document, written in the same normalised '; ' form as the curated author column and feeding it verbatim (ids 191, 193, 194, 196, 202, 203 all have inferred_author identical to author). 47 of 149 rows are populated (102 are NULL/empty, matching inferred_title), and 22 of those hold several authors under the uniform delimiter, e.g. 'Tomonari Dotera; Shinichi Bekku; Primoz Ziherl'. Each element is one author: the same repeating group as author, in its candidate state, and it belongs in the same child relation carried with a source/status marker rather than a delimited string.

subject: original_author
justification: The Author field captured verbatim from pdfinfo and retained for audit against the curated author column - not a list, because its delimiters are incoherent and unparseable: id 94 'Niles Johnsonand Donald Yau' (no separator at all), id 8 comma-delimited, id 98 with a trailing ';', ids 99/103/104 in ', ..., and X' form. Across 149 rows, 55 contain ';', 18 a comma and 12 the word 'and'. The paired original_title confirms the raw-capture role: id 2 keeps the undecoded entity 'Quasicrystals—The impact of N.G. de Bruijn', id 10 is 'PII: S0921-5093(00)01302-2', id 9 has OCR debris spliced mid-title. A column that cannot be split without inventing data is not a repeating group; it is one fact - what the PDF's metadata said.

subject: disposition
justification: 9 adjudicated dependency(ies) violate 3NF under the approved keys: author -> author_source; author -> original_author; original_author -> author; original_author -> author_source (and 5 more). Nothing regenerates this database -- it has no builder and is its own source of truth -- so unlike the generated catalogues the update anomalies are real and the redundancy can drift. Fixing it means migrating the file in place with a lossless proof and a compatibility view, which has not been done. This is the exemption most worth revisiting. Its document-valued columns (author, inferred_author) were separately accepted and are not what blocks it.

subject: *all-unruled*
justification: Every determinant here with even one testing group is ruled individually below; the blanket touches only determinants that hold by rarity. The census: of the 15 unary determinants, 9 have zero repeat groups -- id, path, filename, sha256, text_path, suggested_name, original_filename, original_path, standard_filename, each 1457 distinct in 1457 rows, because one PDF per row makes every naming and hashing column a row serial. The 6 with any repetition (source_subgroup, publication_year, suggested_folder, title_source, title, size_bytes) are all listed individually. All 40 composite determinants contain at least one of the five near-unique columns size_bytes (1456 distinct), inferred_title (1452), text_chars (1446), title (1365), creation_date (1342); not one is free of them. So the blanket closes exactly 45 determinants: 5 zero-repetition naming columns plus 40 near-key composites. Nine further columns are constant ([] -> source_group, topic, pdfinfo_ok, pdfinfo_error, text_ok, text_error, inferred_author, inference_notes, year_source), and the targets a near-key sweeps up are binary or 11- and 26-valued. Those 45 describe a corpus of 1457 distinct files, not the domain.

subject: author -> author_source,original_author
justification: the document's pdfinfo-extracted author attribution -- the single author string lifted from PDF metadata, together with the flag recording whether that lift succeeded owns author_source, original_author. This survives heavy repetition rather than holding by rarity: 939 groups over 1457 rows (0.64) with 70 repeat groups covering 588 rows, including one NULL group of 338. Both targets are mechanical. (a) author_source is a two-valued presence flag: author IS NULL -> 'missing' (338 rows), author IS NOT NULL -> 'pdfinfo' (1119 rows), with zero exceptions -- a stored derived attribute, the same shape as a JSON list owning its own length. (b) author IS original_author on every one of the 1457 rows (0 mismatches); inferred_author is NULL on all 1457 rows and author_source has no 'inferred' value, so the inference lane was never exercised and author is a verbatim copy of original_author. The discriminating test that rules out near-key luck: author does NOT determine publication_year or source_subgroup -- 54 author groups span more than one of each. A determinant that held merely by rarely repeating would have taken those first.

subject: author,creation_date
justification: 1416 distinct groups over 1457 rows (0.97) with only 18 repeat groups covering 59 rows. It contains creation_date, a PDF creation timestamp recorded to the second ('Tue Nov 29 02:08:30 2022 PST') with 1342 distinct values in 1457 rows -- the named timestamp tell. The composite is a near-key and the targets are two-valued (needs_title_review 1208/249, title_source 1208/249), so 18 testing groups separate two classes by chance. Adding an author name to a timestamp does not name a thing that owns a review flag; the document owns both. Note this is the same determinant as 'creation_date,original_author' under a renaming, since author IS original_author on every row -- both yield exactly 1416 groups.

subject: author,text_chars
justification: 1455 distinct groups over 1457 rows (1.00) with a single repeat group of 3 rows. text_chars is an extracted-character count with 1446 distinct values in 1457 rows -- effectively a row serial number. This is the packet's widest claim (7 owned attributes, including original_title with 1116 distinct values) and it is pure sparsity: one testing group cannot establish seven dependencies. The three folder-derived targets are independently disproved -- year_source is 'folder' on all 1457 rows, so publication_year, source_subgroup and suggested_folder are owned by the source directory (DAFx-1998 -> 1998 -> audio/DAFX/DAFx-1998, 26 values each, 1:1), not by an (author, character count) pair. pages has only 11 distinct values, trivially satisfied from 1455 groups.

subject: author_source,creation_date
justification: 1347 distinct groups over 1457 rows (0.92) with 20 repeat groups covering 130 rows. author_source has exactly two values, so this is creation_date alone (1342 distinct in 1457) with a binary tiebreaker -- the near-unique timestamp does all the work. A provenance label paired with a PDF creation instant is not an entity; needs_title_review and title_source are per-document derived flags that the document owns, and they are themselves a single two-valued classification stored twice (see 'needs_title_review').

subject: author_source,inferred_title
justification: 1456 distinct groups over 1457 rows (1.00) -- exactly one repeat group of 2 rows. inferred_title is free text with 1452 distinct values in 1457 rows (fallback filenames such as 'ARF36.PS' where pdfinfo gave nothing), so this determinant is a key in all but one row and determines its targets the way a primary key would. One testing group is no evidence for three dependencies. pages, an 11-value column, is trivially determined at this granularity. This is the same determinant as 'inferred_title,title_source' under a renaming (needs_title_review and title_source are in bijection) -- both yield 1456 groups.

subject: creation_date,original_author
justification: Identical to 'author,creation_date': author IS original_author on all 1457 rows, and both composites yield exactly 1416 groups (0.97) with 18 repeat groups over 59 rows. It holds because creation_date is a second-resolution PDF timestamp with 1342 distinct values, making the pair a near-key. A (timestamp, person name) tuple owns neither the title-review flag nor the title provenance label.

subject: creation_date,pages,producer
justification: 1375 distinct groups over 1457 rows (0.94) with 16 repeat groups covering 98 rows -- a near-key built on the creation_date timestamp (1342 distinct values). The targets are decisively disproved on domain grounds, not just statistics: year_source is 'folder' on all 1457 rows, so publication_year is read from the directory the file was scanned in, and source_subgroup / suggested_folder are that same directory under two other names (26 values each, in exact 1:1 correspondence with publication_year). Those three belong to the source path, which nothing in this determinant names. A (creation instant, page count, producer string) triple is a bookkeeping composite -- producer is the PDF-writer tool with 207 distinct values, and pages has 11.

subject: creation_date,producer
justification: 1351 distinct groups over 1457 rows (0.93) with 18 repeat groups covering 124 rows. creation_date alone already has 1342 distinct values, so producer contributes almost nothing; the pair is a near-key. The single target needs_title_review is binary (1208 zeros, 249 ones), so 18 testing groups separating two classes is what you expect by chance. Neither a timestamp nor the name of the PDF-writing tool owns a human-review flag about a document's title.

subject: creation_date,publication_year
justification: 1348 distinct groups over 1457 rows (0.93) with 20 repeat groups covering 129 rows. publication_year has 26 values and is itself derived from the scan folder (year_source is 'folder' on all 1457 rows), so this is the near-unique creation_date timestamp with a coarse partition attached. The two targets are one binary classification stored twice. Identical in effect to 'creation_date,suggested_folder' -- publication_year and suggested_folder are 1:1 across all 26 values, and both composites yield exactly 1348 groups.

subject: creation_date,suggested_folder
justification: The same determinant as 'creation_date,publication_year' under a renaming: suggested_folder ('audio/DAFX/DAFx-1998') and publication_year (1998) are in exact 1:1 correspondence over 26 values, and both yield 1348 groups over 1457 rows (0.93) with 20 repeat groups. It holds because creation_date is a second-resolution timestamp with 1342 distinct values. A destination folder path plus a creation instant is not a thing that owns needs_title_review or title_source.

Representative of the six naming columns that are exact keys in this instance (filename, text_path, suggested_name, original_filename, original_path, standard_filename -- 1457 distinct each, zero repeat groups). A basename is unique here only because this corpus happens to prefix files by edition; across 26 proceedings folders a repeated basename is ordinary, and only path -- the full path, already the declared key -- is unique by construction. Zero testing groups means zero evidence.

The declared INTEGER PRIMARY KEY and an already-adjudicated intended key of this relation. A surrogate row identifier owns every attribute of the document row by definition, in every legal state, not just this one.

subject: inferred_title,needs_title_review
justification: 1456 distinct groups over 1457 rows (1.00) -- one repeat group of 2 rows. inferred_title is a free-text title with 1452 distinct values in 1457 rows; it is a key in all but one row, so it determines anything at all. needs_title_review adds nothing (2 values). The claimed targets are exactly the ones a near-key sweeps up cheaply: author_source has 2 values and pages has 11. This is the same determinant as 'inferred_title,title_source' -- needs_title_review and title_source are in bijection -- and both yield 1456 groups.

subject: inferred_title,title_source
justification: Identical to 'inferred_title,needs_title_review' (title_source and needs_title_review are two spellings of one binary classification); both yield 1456 groups over 1457 rows with a single repeat group of 2 rows. The determinant is a near-unique free-text column and determines author_source (2 values) and pages (11 values) by never repeating, not because a title string owns an author-extraction provenance label.

subject: needs_title_review -> title_source
justification: title_source currently takes two values and each maps to one flag value, so the flag determines the source only because the source has exactly two possibilities. Add a third source that also needs review -- an XMP title, say -- and needs_title_review=1 maps to two sources at once. The dependency is a bijection in today's value set, not a constraint on legal states. The derivation runs the other way and is ruled separately.

subject: needs_title_review,pages,text_chars
justification: 1454 distinct groups over 1457 rows (1.00) with 2 repeat groups covering 5 rows. text_chars is an extracted-character count with 1446 distinct values -- a de facto row serial. needs_title_review (2 values) and pages (11 values) barely refine it. The single target author_source has 2 values, so two testing groups are worthless as evidence. author_source is a presence flag on author (NULL -> 'missing', otherwise 'pdfinfo'); it belongs to the author attribution, and neither a review flag, a page count, nor a character count names that. Same determinant as 'pages,text_chars,title_source' under the needs_title_review/title_source renaming -- both yield 1454 groups.

subject: original_author -> author,author_source
justification: the document's pdfinfo-extracted author attribution -- the raw author string as PDF metadata reported it; this is the derivation direction (original_author is the source column, author the stored copy) owns author, author_source. Same 939 groups over 1457 rows (0.64), 70 repeat groups covering 588 rows, as 'author' -- necessarily, since the two columns are byte-identical on all 1457 rows (0 mismatches). Read in this direction the mechanism is the builder's copy rule: author = coalesce(inferred_author, original_author), and inferred_author is NULL on all 1457 rows while author_source never takes an 'inferred' value, so the inference lane was never exercised and author collapses to original_author. author_source is the presence flag on that same extraction: NULL -> 'missing' (338), non-NULL -> 'pdfinfo' (1119), exceptionless. The near-key tell does not apply -- original_author fails to determine publication_year or source_subgroup, with 54 groups spanning more than one of each.

subject: original_title -> title_source,needs_title_review
justification: the pdfinfo-supplied title slot -- specifically its presence or absence, which is what the two title-provenance columns record owns title_source, needs_title_review. Intended only on NULL-ness, and only for two of the five claimed attributes. The real rule partitions the whole table: original_title IS NULL -> title_source='filename', needs_title_review=1 (249 rows); original_title IS NOT NULL -> 'pdfinfo', 0 (1208 rows); zero exceptions. The string's value contributes nothing -- all 1116 distinct non-NULL titles map to the same pair -- so this is not the near-key tell despite 1117 groups over 1457 rows. It is also not independent evidence: it is candidate 'needs_title_review' restated with a high-cardinality free-text column in the determinant slot, so do NOT decompose on original_title; the flags belong to the document's title-provenance class. REJECTED here: author, original_author, author_source. Those hold on the NULL side only because all 249 NULL-title rows also lack an author, and on the non-NULL side because of uncorrected template metadata -- the 51 rows sharing 'Proceedings of the 21st International Conference on Digital Audio Effects (DAFx-18)' all carry one author string that is the proceedings/template editor's, not the 51 papers' authors, and the same holds for the DAFx'04, DAFx-02, DAFx 14 and DAFx-22 template groups

subject: pages,text_chars,title_source
justification: The same determinant as 'needs_title_review,pages,text_chars' under a renaming (title_source and needs_title_review are in bijection): both yield 1454 groups over 1457 rows (1.00) with 2 repeat groups covering 5 rows. It holds because text_chars is a near-unique extracted-character count (1446 distinct values). A (page count, character count, provenance label) triple is exactly the bookkeeping composite the brief warns about -- counts and categories identify nothing. The target author_source is a derived presence flag on the author column and belongs with the author attribution.

Declared TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE and the other already-adjudicated intended key. An absolute filesystem path names exactly one catalogued file, so it owns that file's scan record. This is the natural key the whole catalogue is built on.

subject: publication_year -> source_subgroup,suggested_folder
justification: The derived side of the construction ruled intended above, pointing back at its own input. year_source is 'folder' on all 1457 rows: the year was computed from source_subgroup, so the subgroup owns the year and not the reverse. It holds only because this corpus happens to give each year exactly one proceedings folder, and it breaks the moment an edition is split across two folders, or a postponed edition is foldered off its calendar year. A four-digit year is not an entity that owns a scan directory.

The most tempting near-key here, and the schema refutes it in its own words: the database carries duplicate_sets(sha256, count, paths_json), a table whose existence declares that one content hash may cover several paths. That table is empty today, which is exactly why sha256 has 1457 distinct values in 1457 rows and zero repeat groups -- the claim is never tested even once. A content hash cannot own path, id, filename, original_path, suggested_name or standard_filename, which are the location and naming facts the duplicate table exists to hold apart from it.

subject: size_bytes -> needs_title_review,title_source
justification: 1456 distinct byte lengths in 1457 rows: exactly one repeat group, of two rows. Both targets are binary (1208/249), so a single two-row group agreeing is worth nothing -- it would agree by chance about seven times in ten. A file's byte length does not own whether its title needed recovering from the filename.

subject: source_subgroup -> publication_year
justification: the subgroups are named for their years -- DAFx-1998, DAFx-1999 -- and the folder is that name under audio/DAFX/. Both dependents are parses of the subgroup string, so they hold in every legal state and a relation keyed by subgroup would store the year twice, once inside the name and once beside it.

subject: source_subgroup -> publication_year,suggested_folder
justification: source_subgroup names a real entity -- the DAFx proceedings edition the file was scanned out of ('DAFx-1998' ... 'DAFx-2025'). 26 groups over 1457 rows, every group a repeat group, sizes 40 to 82: the maximum possible testing, the opposite of the sparsity tell. Both targets are exact constructions from it, verified on all 1457 rows: suggested_folder = 'audio/DAFX/' || source_subgroup, and publication_year = the trailing year of the subgroup. The builder states the direction itself -- year_source is 'folder' on every row, so the year is read from the scan directory. The edition owns its year and its destination folder.

subject: source_subgroup -> suggested_folder
justification: the subgroups are named for their years -- DAFx-1998, DAFx-1999 -- and the folder is that name under audio/DAFX/. Both dependents are parses of the subgroup string, so they hold in every legal state and a relation keyed by subgroup would store the year twice, once inside the name and once beside it.

subject: suggested_folder -> publication_year,source_subgroup
justification: Same artefact under a renaming, and not accidental by chance: suggested_folder = 'audio/DAFX/' || source_subgroup on all 1457 rows and will keep holding. It is accidental as an ownership claim. suggested_folder is a computed output column, so recovering source_subgroup from it inverts a string concatenation rather than naming an entity that owns an attribute; the construction runs the other way. source_subgroup is the owner, and keying anything on a proposed destination path would record the derivation backwards.

subject: title -> author,author_source,needs_title_review,original_author,original_title,title_source
justification: Free text, 1365 distinct values in 1457 rows, and the eight repeat groups covering 100 rows are not documents sharing a work -- they are proceedings front matter and unedited templates ('Proceedings of the 21st International Conference on Digital Audio Effects (DAFx-18)' x51, "TEMPLATES FOR DAFX'04, Naples, Italy" x19, 'INTRODUCTION' x5). Those rows agree on author because they are copies of one template file, so the agreement is the near-key working, not a title owning an attribution. A free-text title string is a near-key, not an owner.

subject: title_source -> needs_title_review
justification: the flag records whether a title needs review, and it needs review precisely when it came from the filename rather than the PDF metadata. Every title_source maps to exactly one flag value and the derivation runs in this direction. Intended; the remedy is to derive the flag rather than store it.

subject: model
value: One row is one PDF file currently present in the local reference tree, carrying its extraction status, its raw and curated bibliographic metadata, its intake provenance, and its proposed filing location.
justification: The DDL declares id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY and path TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE: a surrogate and the file's current location. Every other unique column is derived and may legally collide. path spans five roots (research-pdfs 68, geometry/Zorin 61, uncategorized 12, geometry/reference-manuals 5, tiling/hat-spectre 3), so equal basenames in different directories are legal - filename, suggested_name and standard_filename are proposals, not identities; ids 189/190 share a sha256 and a title and are separated only by a hand-added ' v2'. original_path/original_filename record intake provenance, and 47 rows point into the reused staging directory .local/references/intake/, which one file can supply twice and which is refilled over time. text_path is a derived sidecar, declared nullable and paired with text_ok/text_error for failed extraction. sha256 is not a key: 148 distinct values over 149 rows, which is exactly why duplicate_sets exists. Scope is current-state - path -> sha256/size_bytes/pages holds only for the file presently at that path, there is no scan or version column, and ids run to 229 over 149 rows, showing rows are curated and deleted in place.

subject: author
justification: delimiter is ambiguous in this data; a splitter would corrupt values silently

subject: inferred_author
justification: empty: not a flat set of scalars

subject: source_subgroup -> publication_year
justification: publication_year is computed from source_subgroup within the row, so the redundancy goes away by deriving it rather than by building a relation keyed by every distinct source_subgroup.

subject: source_subgroup -> suggested_folder
justification: suggested_folder is computed from source_subgroup within the row, so the redundancy goes away by deriving it rather than by building a relation keyed by every distinct source_subgroup.

subject: title_source -> needs_title_review
justification: needs_title_review is computed from title_source within the row, so the redundancy goes away by deriving it rather than by building a relation keyed by every distinct title_source.

subject: model
value: One row is one content hash that two or more catalogued files share, together with the size of that duplicate group and the list of member paths.
justification: The DDL declares sha256 TEXT PRIMARY KEY. SQLite leaves that nullable on a rowid table, but the author's intent is plain: the hash identifies the duplicate group, and count and paths_json are derived facts about it (count = len(paths_json)). count and paths_json look unique only because the table holds exactly one row; a second collision of two files would repeat count = 2 immediately, so both are accidental, and the reported 'constant column -> X' BCNF violations are a one-row artifact. The single row is sha256 1a1c2123..., whose two paths are documents ids 189 and 190, byte-identical copies of 'A chiral aperiodic monotile' - the only collision among 149 rows with 148 distinct hashes. A sibling catalog builder, /home/wreckoning90125/polytwister-native/tools/build_hopf_lens_catalog.py (not this authority's builder - its columns are source_count/source_ids_json), inserts into its same-named table only when len(source_ids) > 1, corroborating 'hash shared by two or more files' as the entity. paths_json is a member list kept as one derived group value; no atomicity subject was raised for it. Scope is current-state: an aggregate over the inventory as it stands, recomputed on rescan.
